Metrics by Funnel Stage

Stage metrics are usually taught as a diagnostic: find the leaking stage, fix it. The expert use is almost the opposite — to bound, before any work begins, how much the funnel could possibly be worth, and to recognise the cases where the answer is "not enough, so the problem is somewhere else entirely."

1. Two rooms, five weeks apart

On the morning of 4 February 2026, Devika Raghunath had ninety minutes and one number she did not want to say out loud. She was VP of Growth at Oormila Money, a five-year-old Bengaluru investing app with twenty-two lakh registered users, competing for the same first-time equity and mutual-fund investor that Groww, Zerodha and Angel One had been converting at scale since the pandemic. The finance committee, chaired by the independent director Suhas Deshpande with the CFO Nandita Rao beside him, had asked a narrow question: should Oormila's ₹18.4 crore quarterly performance-marketing budget be renewed, cut, or reallocated? Devika's team reported customer acquisition cost as ₹292. That figure was arithmetically correct — ₹18.4 crore divided by the 6.3 lakh accounts created in the October-to-December quarter — and it was, she had concluded over the previous fortnight, close to meaningless. Only 1.04 lakh of those accounts had completed know-your-customer verification and funded a first deposit. Only 42,000 had transacted a second time within sixty days. Measured against a funded account, CAC was ₹1,769. Measured against a customer who behaved like a customer, it was ₹4,381. Blended lifetime contribution, on the company's own twenty-four-month model, was ₹803.

What made the meeting hard was not that the numbers were bad. It was that Devika could not yet say which of three very different stories they supported. The first story was operational: a single regulated step in the middle of the journey, KYC completion, was converting at 63.4 percent when the company's own best-performing segment achieved 81 percent, and fixing it would move everything downstream. The second story was about mix: two-thirds of the quarter's signups had arrived through broad social and video campaigns bought on a cost-per-install basis, and those users were structurally different from the search-intent users who had dominated the previous quarter. The third story was the one nobody in growth wants to tell a board — that no achievable combination of stage improvements could close a gap of that size, and the honest recommendation was to cut spend and change what the company charged for. Stage metrics were the only instrument that could distinguish the three, and the distinction was worth roughly ₹40 crore over the following financial year.

Five weeks later and 840 kilometres away, on 11 March 2026, Meera Chandrasekhar faced a differently shaped version of the same problem in a low-ceilinged conference room at Onkar Systems in Pune. Onkar sold shop-floor quality intelligence to mid-market auto-component manufacturers: an edge gateway that sat on the plant network reading data off programmable logic controllers, plus a subscription analytics layer that flagged process drift before it became scrap. Annual recurring revenue was ₹58 crore across 190 customers, average contract value ₹30 lakh, and the company had just been asked by its board to approve ₹9 crore to build a product-led trial motion — the self-serve, try-before-you-buy funnel that the board's newest member had watched work at a horizontal SaaS company. Meera, who ran the new motion, had spent three weeks reconstructing the last four quarters of Onkar's funnel and had found something that made the ₹9 crore look like the wrong answer to a correctly identified problem. Marketing-qualified leads had tripled year on year to 1,240 in the December quarter. Bookings had not moved. The stage where the funnel broke was not a page, a form or a price — it was a queue. Onkar had nine field engineers who could commission twenty-two gateways a month, and sixty-one signed pilots waiting for a slot.

Both executives were about to discover the same thing from opposite directions: that the value of stage-level measurement lies less in finding the low number than in establishing what the whole system is capable of, and that the discipline most often earns its keep by telling a growth team to stop working on growth.

2. The idea, its lineage, and the fights inside it

Stated precisely, measuring by funnel stage means defining a sequence of mutually exclusive, timestamped states that a prospect occupies on the way to becoming a repeat customer; assigning to each transition a conditional probability estimated over a cohort observed for a fixed window; and reporting each transition separately, with its own denominator, its own owner and its own intervention set. The three italicised commitments — mutually exclusive states, conditional probabilities, fixed observation windows — are what separate a funnel model from a pile of dashboards. Almost every pathology described later in this note is a violation of one of them.

The lineage is older than software and less coherent than it is usually presented. Elias St. Elmo Lewis's attention-interest-desire sequence, circulating in American advertising trade press from 1898, was a theory of a salesman's talk track, not a measurement system. Frank Hutchinson Dukesmith added "conviction" in 1904; Edward Strong codified AIDA in The Psychology of Selling in 1925. The first genuinely measurement-oriented version arrived in 1961, and arrived twice: Robert Lavidge and Gary Steiner's hierarchy-of-effects model in the Journal of Marketing, and Russell Colley's DAGMAR report for the Association of National Advertisers, whose entire argument was that advertising objectives must be stated as movements between defined, measurable communication states rather than as sales. Colley is the direct intellectual ancestor of every stage-conversion dashboard in use today, and his central claim — that you cannot hold a stage accountable for an outcome two stages downstream — is still the most frequently violated principle in the field.

The software-era rewrite came from Dave McClure's 2007 "Startup Metrics for Pirates", which moved three of the five stages inside the product (acquisition, activation, retention, referral, revenue) and thereby moved ownership from marketing to engineering; and from Sean Ellis's growth-hacking practice at Dropbox and LogMeIn shortly after, which added the insistence that each stage be run as a stream of controlled experiments. Both were practitioner frameworks, not research programmes, and both were absorbed into the digital-first growth electives now taught at INSEAD, HKUST and Cambridge in a metrics-led rather than tactics-led form.

Where a near-expert differs from a competent practitioner is in knowing that this consensus is contested on its foundations, not merely on its details. Four positions are worth being able to state in the form each camp would actually endorse.

An expert holds the arithmetic tightly and the interpretation loosely.

3. Mechanics in depth, including the parts usually left implicit

Begin with the structure of the object. Figure 1 shows Oormila Money's December-quarter funnel drawn the way an expert draws it — with the uninstrumented population explicitly on the page, because the single most common error in reading a funnel is forgetting that its widest bar is not the top of anything.

The first implicit step is choosing how many stages to have. Practitioners treat this as a discovery exercise ("let us map the journey"), but it is a design decision with a hard constraint: the correct number of stages is the number of distinct interventions the organisation can actually run against, staffed and sequenced, within one planning cycle. Oormila could have drawn fourteen states — Devika's first draft had eleven — but the company had four teams capable of independent action, so a seven-stage model already exceeded its capacity to act and mostly generated additional meetings. The tell that a funnel has too many stages is that at least one transition has never had an experiment run against it in eighteen months.

The second implicit step is identity resolution at each boundary, and it is where most funnels quietly become fiction. A click that cannot be joined to an install, or an install that cannot be joined to an account, forces the analyst to compare two independently measured population totals and call the ratio a conversion rate. It is not one: it is a ratio of two aggregates over overlapping but non-identical populations, and it is systematically biased whenever the two populations have different observation windows. After Apple's app-tracking changes and the corresponding tightening on Android, the click-to-install join at Oormila was probabilistic for roughly 38 percent of iOS traffic, which meant the 26.9 percent in Figure 1 carried an uncertainty band no dashboard displayed.

The arithmetic that actually matters

Write end-to-end conversion as the product of the transitions, and acquisition cost as spend divided by that product:

CAC = S / (V × r1 × r2 × … × rk), where S is spend, V is top-of-funnel volume, and ri is the conditional probability of surviving transition i.

Take logarithms and differentiate. The elasticity of CAC with respect to any ri is exactly −1, for every i, without exception. A ten percent relative improvement in the click-to-install rate and a ten percent relative improvement in KYC completion have identical effects on CAC. At Oormila this is easy to verify: lifting KYC completion from 63.4 to 69.7 percent (a ten percent relative gain) raises funded accounts from 1.04 lakh to 1.144 lakh and drops CAC from ₹1,769 to ₹1,608; lifting click-to-install from 26.9 to 29.6 percent produces the same ₹1,608.

This single result demolishes the most widely taught heuristic in the field — "find the stage with the worst conversion and fix that one." The worst stage has no special claim on your attention. What differs across stages is not leverage but two other quantities: headroom, the distance between the current rate and a realistically attainable ceiling, and cost of movement, the engineering, regulatory and margin cost of closing that distance. The expert's selection rule is to rank stages by expected relative lift per rupee of cost, adjusted for confidence, and to be indifferent to where in the funnel they sit.

Table 2 is where the case turns, and it is worth dwelling on why. If every one of the five CAC-relevant targets is hit, simultaneously, inside ninety days — an outcome no growth team in Devika's experience had ever actually achieved — Oormila's acquisition cost falls to ₹1,165 against a lifetime contribution of ₹864. The company is still twenty-six percent underwater. Devika could compute an even more generous bound by assuming every stage hit its best-decile rate at once, which gives 2.69 lakh funded accounts and a CAC of ₹684, marginally below LTV. But that frontier is unattainable in principle, not merely in practice: the best-decile rates were observed in different segments, and the mix that produces the best click-to-install rate is not the mix that produces the best funding rate. Stacking best-of-breed segment rates into a single forecast is the most common way a growth plan lies to a board.

The technique has a name worth learning: bounding the prize. Before committing headcount, compute the CAC and LTV that would obtain under a deliberately optimistic but internally consistent scenario. If the optimistic scenario still fails the business test, the funnel is not the problem, and every hour spent optimising it is an hour not spent on pricing, on channel mix, or on the product's underlying value. This is the reasoning that carried Devika's recommendation, and it is the single most valuable thing stage metrics do that no other instrument does as cheaply.

Second-order effects the arithmetic hides

Three matter enough to state formally. First, conditioning: each rate is a conditional probability, and improving an upstream rate changes the population that arrives downstream. If the install-to-account rate rises because a friction point was removed, the additional accounts are, on average, lower-intent than the ones that were already converting, and the account-to-KYC rate will fall. A downstream rate declining after an upstream win is frequently evidence of success, not failure — the diagnostic is whether the downstream count rose while its rate fell.

Second, statistical resolution decays down the funnel. The number of observations needed per arm to detect a change of δ in a rate p, at conventional 95 percent confidence and 80 percent power, is approximately 16p(1−p)/δ². At Oormila's KYC-completion stage, where 4.1 lakh users enter per quarter, detecting a one-point absolute change on a 63.4 percent base needs about 37,000 per arm — trivially affordable. At the D365 retention stage for a single acquisition channel, where the denominator is roughly 8,000 per quarter and the base rate is 22 percent, detecting a three-point change needs about 3,050 per arm, which is affordable in sample but takes a year to read out. The stages with the most economic weight are almost always the stages with the least statistical resolution and the longest latency, which is why experts build validated surrogate endpoints — an early observable, such as time-to-second-transaction, whose correlation with the twelve-month endpoint has itself been established on historical cohorts before being trusted.

Third, Goodhart pressure at the seams. Give a team a stage rate as its objective and it will optimise its own numerator by degrading the next stage's denominator. The classic mechanism is an incentivised install campaign: the interest-stage team doubles installs and improves nothing, while the transaction team's conversion rate halves through no action of its own and becomes accountable for a decline it did not cause. This is not a motivational problem; it is a structural consequence of assigning conditional probabilities to independent owners, and it is managed by making at least one team accountable for a joint rate that spans a seam.

4. When the framework applies, and when it actively misleads

The conditions can be stated as four testable claims, each of which either holds or does not for a given business.

Claim one: the states are mutually exclusive and ordered. A user who is in state four cannot simultaneously be in state two, and cannot reach state four without passing through state three. At Oormila this holds almost perfectly, because the states are enforced by regulation and by software: you cannot fund an account you have not KYC'd. At Onkar it holds badly. A plant head who has seen the product at a trade show, spoken informally to a peer at another firm, and then received a cold email is in three states at once, and Onkar's CRM records whichever one a sales executive typed last. When ordering fails, stage rates become an artefact of data entry, and the correct response is to collapse the model to the two or three boundaries that are genuinely enforced by an artefact — a signed document, a shipped device, a payment — rather than by a judgement.

Claim two: transitions are approximately stationary over the measurement window. Stage rates are only forecastable if the mechanism generating them is stable. Oormila's December quarter violated this: the mix of acquisition channels shifted so sharply that the blended signup-to-funded rate fell while every underlying segment rate rose. Claim three: the transitions are the binding constraint. Stage metrics presume that conversion is limited by persuasion and friction. Where conversion is limited by capacity, the entire framework misleads, because the rate is a function of queue length rather than of anything a designer can change. This is precisely Onkar's situation, and it is common in any business with a physical, human or regulated fulfilment step: field installation, medical devices, lending underwriting, immigration-adjacent services. The diagnostic is to plot the stage rate against the queue depth in the preceding period; if the correlation is strongly negative, you have a capacity problem wearing a conversion problem's clothing.

Claim four: attributed conversions are incremental. This one is almost never true and is the reason Devika commissioned a geo-holdout across fourteen districts in December 2025. Suppressing all Oormila paid media in the holdout districts and comparing against matched controls showed that 31 percent of last-click-attributed funded accounts arrived anyway. On branded search specifically — ₹3.2 crore of spend, 26,000 attributed funded accounts — the non-incremental share was 78 percent. The implied cost of the genuinely incremental accounts from branded search was ₹5,594 each, against a lifetime contribution of ₹803. No amount of stage-level optimisation could rescue that line; it simply had to stop.

5. Hard edge cases and what happens at the organisational seams

Two-sided and marketplace. Omkara Bazaar, a Surat-based wholesale apparel marketplace connecting mills to small-town retailers, runs two funnels whose stages are coupled by a quantity neither side owns. A retailer's search-to-order rate is not a property of the retailer funnel at all; it is determined by whether a mill has listed the right fabric in the right quantity that week. Omkara Bazaar's demand funnel looked healthy for two quarters while its search fill rate — the share of buyer searches returning at least three in-stock listings above a minimum rating — fell from 71 to 48 percent. The demand team read the falling search-to-order rate as a ranking-relevance problem and spent a quarter on the search algorithm. The correct instrument in a marketplace is a coupled stage rate: every demand-side transition should be reported conditioned on the supply state at the moment it occurred, so that a rate is never blamed on the side that did not cause it.

Regulated. Oormila's KYC step is a stage that the growth organisation cannot own, cannot A/B test freely, and cannot remove. Its conversion rate is a joint function of a third-party vendor's optical character recognition quality, the customer's document availability, SEBI and RBI process requirements, and network conditions in tier-three towns. The distinctive failure is organisational: because compliance owns the requirement and product owns the screen, no one owns the rate. Mature regulated companies handle this by naming a single accountable owner for the regulated transition and giving that person a budget, which is a governance answer rather than an analytical one. What they say they do is "collaborate across functions"; what actually works is a name on a line.

Hardware plus software. Onkar's funnel contains a stage measured in trucks. Between "pilot signed" and "pilot running" sits gateway shipment, plant-network whitelisting, PLC protocol mapping and an on-site commissioning visit — a transition with a mean latency of thirty-one days, a variance larger than its mean, and a marginal cost of roughly ₹48,000 per attempt. Conversion at this stage is not elastic to messaging at all. It is elastic to engineer-hours. Companies with a physical stage should report it with a capacity denominator alongside the demand denominator: "38 of 61 signed pilots commissioned" is a conversion rate, but "38 of 47 available commissioning slots consumed" is the number that tells you whether to hire.

AI-native. Omkara Intelligence, a Mumbai company selling a contract-review assistant to in-house legal teams, discovered that the usual activation definition — did the user perform the action — is the wrong shape for a probabilistic product. The same user performing the same action twice can have a good experience and a bad one, because the model's output quality varies. Activation in an AI product must be acceptance-weighted: not "uploaded five documents" but "exported a reviewed clause set into a live client document." There is a second asymmetry. In a conventional funnel, more engagement at a stage is unambiguously good; in an inference-metered product, engagement carries a marginal cost, so each stage needs a cost metric reported beside its conversion rate. A funnel that reports only rates will happily optimise a company into negative gross margin.

Multi-product. When a company sells several products to the same account, the funnel branches, and the branch point is usually mismodelled. A cross-sell customer does not re-enter at awareness; they enter at something like stage four, with a materially different conversion profile, and mixing them into the new-customer denominator flatters every rate downstream. The workable convention is to maintain a separate funnel per product with an explicit "entered from existing relationship" flag, and to never report a blended new-plus-cross-sell conversion rate without the flag's split alongside it.

6. Ten nuances that separate an expert from a competent practitioner

The worst stage is not the best stage to fix. Because CAC has unit elasticity to every transition, leverage is uniform and only headroom and cost differ. The tell-tale sign is the question an expert asks first in a funnel review: not "which number is lowest" but "what is the highest rate anyone has ever observed here, in any segment, and what did it cost them." The obvious reading is wrong because a low rate frequently reflects an irreducible feature of the category — Oormila's 40 percent KYC-to-funded rate looks alarming beside a retail checkout rate of 70 percent, but funding an investment account requires a bank transfer and a decision to part with savings, and no interface change makes that a 70 percent behaviour.

Precision decays as economic weight increases. The transitions that determine whether a business works — retention at nine months, expansion at renewal — sit at the narrow end of the funnel, where denominators are smallest and readouts slowest. The tell-tale sign is an experiment roadmap densely populated at the top and empty below the transaction stage. Experts respond not by running underpowered tests but by constructing and validating surrogate endpoints, and by being explicit that a surrogate is a claim requiring evidence: before trusting "time-to-second-transaction" as a proxy for twelve-month value, Oormila's analytics lead in Hyderabad, Priya Menon, had to show that the relationship held across three historical cohorts and did not break when the acquisition mix changed.

The blended rate is a statement about mix, not about mechanism. Table 3's paradox is not a curiosity; it is the default condition of any company whose channel mix is moving, which is every growing company. The tell-tale sign is a rate that moves sharply in a period when nothing shipped. An expert asks for the mix table before the rate table, every time, and refuses to discuss a blended movement until the segment decomposition is on the screen.

A falling downstream rate can be the receipt for an upstream win. Conditional probabilities are defined over populations that upstream changes deliberately alter. When Onkar's marketing team tripled MQLs, the MQL-to-sales-accepted rate fell from 51 to 35 percent — and sales-accepted leads still rose in absolute terms from 388 to 430. The tell-tale sign is a rate falling while the count rises. The obvious reading — "marketing is sending junk" — is sometimes true and is unfalsifiable from the rate alone; the discriminating test is whether the downstream-most count, the one closest to revenue, also rose.

Denominator maturity is a reporting decision with a right answer. Reporting a thirty-day repeat rate on a cohort acquired eighteen days ago is not conservative, it is wrong, and it biases downward by a predictable amount. The tell-tale sign is a monthly retention chart whose most recent point is always the worst one. Experts report only fully matured cohorts in trend lines and place immature cohorts in a visually distinct, explicitly labelled region — and they know that this single convention eliminates roughly half of all false retention alarms.

Under a growth ramp, blended retention falls even when retention improves. If acquisition is growing thirty percent quarter on quarter, the proportion of the active base that is young rises, and since young cohorts always retain worse than old ones, the blended figure declines mechanically. The tell-tale sign is a retention decline that tracks the acquisition growth rate with a one-quarter lag. The obvious reading — "the product is getting worse" — is a composition artefact, and the correction is to report retention normalised by cohort age, never as a base-wide average.

Most "magic numbers" are selection, not causation. The observation that users who do X in week one retain far better is almost always a fact about who chooses to do X, not about what doing X causes. The tell-tale sign is a correlation of implausible size — a four-fold retention difference — attached to an action that takes thirty seconds. Experts demand the forced-exposure experiment before building a product around the correlation, and they know that the experiment usually shows an effect an order of magnitude smaller than the correlation implied. This is the mistake that cost Omkara Intelligence a quarter, described in section 8.

Latency is a metric, not a nuisance. Two funnels with identical conversion rates but different time-to-convert distributions behave completely differently under a spend ramp, under a cash constraint, and under a capacity constraint. The tell-tale sign is a funnel report containing no histograms. Onkar's pilot-to-contract transition had a median of 41 days and a ninetieth percentile of 138 days; a quarterly conversion report computed on calendar quarters therefore mixed three different acquisition vintages in every cell, and the apparent quarter-on-quarter movements were largely an artefact of when deals happened to land.

The funnel's widest bar is not the top of the market. Everything to the left of Figure 1's first stage — the people who saw an ad and formed a negative view, the people the media plan never reached, the people who were in-market last month — is invisible to the instrumentation and is usually much larger than everything inside it. The tell-tale sign is a growth plan that proposes to improve conversion by forty percent and makes no claim at all about reach. This is the Ehrenberg-Bass critique in its operationally useful form: a company that optimises only the instrumented region can win every stage and still lose the category, and the only corrective is external measurement — brand trackers, category panels, unaided-recall studies — that the funnel cannot generate from its own data.

Stage metrics are the cheapest instrument for deciding not to act. Bounding the prize, as in Table 2, takes an analyst two days and can save a quarter of engineering time. The tell-tale sign of an expert is that they run this calculation before the roadmap conversation rather than after it, and that they are visibly willing to conclude that the funnel is not worth working on. Competent practitioners use funnels to justify projects; experts use them to kill projects, which is both rarer and more valuable.

7. How the picture changes by product type and company stage

Begin with what does not change, because the honest answer is: more than most treatments admit. The multiplicative identity holds everywhere. The unit-elasticity result holds everywhere. Simpson's paradox, denominator maturity, the growth-ramp composition effect and the selection-versus-causation trap are invariant across consumer, business-to-business, marketplace, hardware and AI products, and a practitioner who has internalised those five ideas transfers almost completely between categories. What changes is the vocabulary, the latency, and the identity of the binding constraint.

In consumer products the entire funnel can complete within one session, latency is measured in minutes, sample sizes are large enough that almost any stage can be tested properly, and the binding constraint is usually attention. In business-to-business and enterprise the unit of analysis shifts from person to account, which breaks the mutual-exclusivity assumption badly — at Onkar, a single deal involved a plant manager, a quality head, an IT security reviewer and a finance controller, each at a different point in their own journey, and the "account stage" is a lossy projection of four individual states onto one. Latency stretches to quarters, sample sizes collapse to dozens, and formal experimentation becomes largely infeasible, so the honest practice is qualitative loss analysis on every lost deal rather than pseudo-rigorous stage tests on samples of thirty. Loyalty ceases to be a repeat-purchase count and becomes net revenue retention, which is a currency-weighted rather than a person-weighted metric and therefore obeys different arithmetic entirely.

Marketplaces add the coupling described above. Hardware adds a capacity-constrained physical stage and a non-trivial cost per conversion attempt, which means the marketplace and hardware cases share a feature that pure software lacks: conversion can be too high for the system to serve, and the growth team's job includes throttling demand. AI-native products add output-quality variance inside each transition and a marginal cost per engagement, requiring every stage rate to be paired with a cost and an acceptance measure.

Company stage changes the correct level of granularity, and the mistake runs in both directions. An early-stage company with two thousand monthly signups cannot support seven stages; its rates are dominated by noise, and the right discipline is three stages watched obsessively with qualitative follow-up on every individual failure. A late-stage company can support fine-grained decomposition but acquires the opposite pathology — stage proliferation, where the number of tracked transitions exceeds the number of teams able to act on them, producing dashboards that describe the business beautifully and change it not at all. Onkar, at ₹58 crore of recurring revenue, sat exactly at the crossover: large enough to need real stage discipline, small enough that its nine-stage CRM model had four transitions no one had ever run an intervention against.

8. Three worked examples, including one that failed

Oormila Money: the stage nobody owned

The KYC-initiated-to-completed transition at 63.4 percent was Oormila's largest single pocket of headroom, and the reason it had persisted for six quarters was structural. The vendor was selected by compliance on the basis of regulatory robustness and per-check price; the screen was built by product; the traffic arriving at it was shaped by growth; and the rate itself appeared on nobody's objectives. When Priya Menon decomposed it, the failure was not uniform: completion in the eight largest cities ran at 79 percent, and in tier-three towns at 44 percent, with the gap concentrated almost entirely in a single step where the vendor's liveness check required a stable video upload. Oormila's own best-decile segment — Bengaluru users on Wi-Fi, iOS, daytime — hit 81 percent, which is where Table 2's ceiling came from. The fix was not a growth fix: it was a vendor migration to a provider supporting an offline-capable, lower-bitrate flow with DigiLocker-based document retrieval, at ₹1.1 crore a year and a quarter of engineering. Expected effect: completion to 74 percent, funded accounts up 16.7 percent relative, CAC from ₹1,769 to ₹1,516 on that lever alone. Devika's contribution was not discovering the number — the number had been on a dashboard for two years — but assigning it an owner and attaching a budget to it.

Omkara Intelligence: optimising the right metric into the ground

The analysis turned up a spectacular correlation: users who ran five or more documents through the reviewer in their first week retained at 71 percent at day ninety, against 18 percent for everyone else. The team declared five-documents-in-week-one the activation metric and, in October, shipped a mandatory onboarding wizard, an in-app nag sequence and a free credit grant designed to force the behaviour.

The intervention moved its target metric by twenty-eight points and made the business worse on every measure that mattered. The diagnosis had two parts. The first was the selection fallacy: users with five real contracts to review in week one were users with a live, funded legal workload, and manufacturing the behaviour did not manufacture the workload. The second was specific to AI products: forcing document uploads consumed model tokens on documents nobody cared about, tripling inference cost per signup and destroying seventeen points of gross margin — a cost that a funnel reporting only conversion rates was structurally incapable of seeing.

The recovery, run between January and April 2026, is more instructive than the failure. Kabir collapsed the nine stages to four, on the principle that a stage without an owner and an intervention is a liability. He redefined activation in acceptance-weighted terms: not an action the user took but an output the model produced that the user accepted and shipped. He ran a randomised holdout on the nag sequence with 2,100 users per arm — powered to detect a five-point change on a 34 percent base, which requires about 1,436 per arm — and measured a −1.9 point effect on day-ninety retention, whereupon the sequence was killed. And he attached a cost metric to every transition, so that inference cost per activated user appeared on the same row as the conversion rate. By April the acceptance-weighted activation rate stood at 19 percent against a pre-intervention 17, day-ninety retention at 38 percent against 34, and gross margin had recovered to 68 percent. The lesson Kabir drew, and repeated to every new analyst since, was that a funnel metric is a hypothesis about causation dressed as a description of behaviour, and that the dressing is what makes it dangerous.

9. Failure modes, their early warning signs, and the cost of late detection

Optimising a correlated proxy. Early warning: the metric moves further and faster than any plausible mechanism would predict. Diagnostic question: has anyone run a forced-exposure experiment on this behaviour, and what was the effect size relative to the observed correlation? Cost of catching late: a quarter of product work, plus the harder cost of having trained the organisation to trust a number that was never load-bearing. Omkara Intelligence caught it in eleven weeks and still lost seventeen points of margin.

Mix shift read as mechanism change. Early warning: a rate moves in a period when no relevant change shipped. Diagnostic question: show me the same rate for each acquisition segment, with each segment's share of volume, for both periods. Cost of catching late: an intervention aimed at a mechanism that was never broken, and — considerably worse — a decision to cut the channel whose rate appeared to fall, which is usually the channel that was growing.

Capacity misread as conversion. Early warning: a stage rate declines monotonically while upstream volume rises. Diagnostic question: plot this rate against queue depth in the preceding period; is the correlation strongly negative? Cost of catching late: at Onkar, roughly ₹2.1 crore of contract value per quarter, compounding as the queue lengthened, plus the reputational cost of pilots abandoned by frustrated plant heads who will not take a second call.

Attribution mistaken for incrementality. Early warning: the sum of channel-attributed conversions exceeds total conversions, or a channel's attributed CAC is implausibly low. Diagnostic question: what is the result of the most recent geo or audience holdout on this channel, and when was it run? Cost of catching late: Oormila spent ₹3.2 crore in a quarter on branded search whose genuinely incremental cost per funded account was ₹5,594 against a lifetime contribution of ₹803 — a loss of roughly ₹2.7 crore per quarter, sustained for five quarters before the holdout was run.

Seam disagreement left unresolved. Early warning: two functions quote different values for the same-named metric in the same meeting and neither is willing to concede. Diagnostic question: which event, at which timestamp, in which system, defines this stage boundary — and who owns that definition? Cost of catching late: not usually money directly, but decision paralysis; the most expensive version is a board that stops believing any growth number, after which every proposal is evaluated on rhetoric.

Stage proliferation. Early warning: a funnel review lasts ninety minutes and produces no decision. Diagnostic question: for each transition, name the team that owns it and the last experiment run against it. Cost of catching late: the slow conversion of an analytics function into a reporting function, which is very hard to reverse because the dashboards become artefacts of organisational identity.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

Four disagreements in this area are live, and none of them is resolved by the evidence currently available.

Do the interior stages exist? The Ehrenberg-Bass position, argued most forcefully by Byron Sharp, is that the sequence awareness → interest → desire → action describes nothing in any buyer's head; buyers are mostly light, mostly loyal to a repertoire rather than a brand, and mostly buy what is mentally and physically available at the moment of need. The evidence is strong and replicated across categories and decades: double jeopardy, the Dirichlet distribution of repeat purchase, and the persistent finding that brand growth comes from penetration rather than loyalty. The instrumented-funnel camp's reply is that the software funnel does not claim to describe mental states at all — its stages are enforced by the product's own state machine, and a user who has not completed KYC genuinely cannot fund an account. The disagreement would be resolved against the funnel camp if it could be shown that interventions at intermediate software stages produce no durable effect on final purchase once selection is controlled for; it would be resolved against Ehrenberg-Bass if penetration-focused reach spending reliably underperformed stage-targeted spending in head-to-head incrementality tests. Both experiments are run constantly and both produce mixed results.

Are funnels or loops the right primitive? Brian Balfour's argument is that a funnel is a one-shot object: you put people in the top and they fall out of the bottom, and the model contains no mechanism by which today's customers produce tomorrow's. A loop — a referral loop, a user-generated-content loop, a paid loop where revenue funds further acquisition — has a cycle time and a coefficient, and compounds. The funnel camp replies that every loop decomposes into a sequence of transitions, and that you cannot improve a loop without knowing which of its transitions is weakest, so the loop is the strategy and the funnel is the instrument. What would resolve it: if companies that manage by loop metrics systematically outgrow matched companies managing by stage metrics, the loop camp wins; the difficulty is that the businesses with strong loops are the businesses with strong products, and no one has managed to separate the two.

Is stage measurement even identified? The incrementality school's strongest form is uncomfortable: every stage conversion rate is a correlation over a self-selected population, and the only quantities with causal content are those produced by randomisation or credible quasi-experiment. On this view most funnel dashboards are elaborate descriptions of who chose what, dressed as a theory of what works. The counter is practical rather than philosophical — a company cannot randomise its KYC requirement, cannot randomise its commissioning queue, and must make decisions weekly on non-experimental evidence. The honest middle position, and the one both Devika and Meera adopted, is that stage metrics are for locating and bounding, and experiments are for deciding: use the funnel to choose what to test, never to conclude what works.

Should the funnel be short or long? A minority but serious position holds that beyond three or four stages, the marginal stage costs more in definitional overhead, seam disputes and false precision than it returns in diagnostic power. The opposing view is that granularity is what makes a stage actionable — "activation" is not a thing a team can work on, whereas "completes liveness check on a 2G connection" is. The evidence is anecdotal on both sides. What is not in dispute is the direction of the error at each extreme: too few stages hides the mechanism, too many hides the decision.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has merely studied this topic arrives at a funnel review with the stage rates. Someone who has internalised it arrives with four things: the mix decomposition behind every rate that moved, the cohort maturity of every number on the page, the bounded prize for the whole funnel under an optimistic scenario, and a proposal about which single transition to test next and why — chosen on headroom and cost, not on being the lowest number. They will be comfortable saying that the funnel is not the constraint, and comfortable saying that they do not know whether an observed correlation is causal. They will have read the retention curve rather than the retention point, and will know that two cohorts can invert their ranking between day thirty and day one-eighty, as Figure 3 shows. They will resist the request to add a stage more often than they accede to it. And they will treat every stage metric as provisional in a specific way: as a hypothesis about where a mechanism lives, awaiting an experiment that will more often disconfirm than confirm it.

12. What each of them decided

Devika Raghunath did not defend the ₹18.4 crore and did not propose cutting it wholesale. She presented Table 2 and the bounded prize first, before any tactical recommendation, and told the finance committee plainly that even a fully successful ninety-day programme across five transitions would leave Oormila at ₹1,165 CAC against ₹864 of lifetime contribution — that the funnel could not, under any honest assumption, be made to work at the current monetisation. Her recommendation had three parts. Cut ₹3.2 crore of branded-search spend outright on the strength of the December holdout, which she committed to re-run in June rather than treating as settled. Fund the KYC vendor migration at ₹1.1 crore a year and name Iqbal Shaikh, the head of compliance, as the single accountable owner of the KYC completion rate, with the rate on his objectives. And take the remaining ₹14 crore of quarterly spend to the product and pricing committee rather than the growth roadmap, because the gap she had bounded was a monetisation gap, not a conversion gap. Suhas Deshpande's summary of the meeting, recorded in the minutes, was that the growth team had been asked to defend a budget and had instead defined a different question.

Meera Chandrasekhar told her board that she did not want the ₹9 crore, or at least not in that shape. She proposed ₹1.4 crore to hire ten commissioning engineers and to build a remote-commissioning firmware path that would let roughly a third of installations be completed without a site visit; ₹2 crore for a genuinely software-only evaluation tier that read a customer's existing PLC data exports and so removed the hardware stage entirely for the subset of plants already logging to a historian; and a deferral of the remainder pending evidence that demand, not capacity, was binding. She also changed the funnel itself, adding "commissioning slot reserved" as an explicit stage reported against a capacity denominator rather than a demand denominator — a single line item that made the constraint visible to everyone in the company every week. Her closing argument was that Onkar had spent a year buying leads at ₹4,097 to fill a queue, and that the cheapest growth available to the company was to stop losing the pilots it had already sold.

Question 1 Devika bounded the prize and concluded the funnel was not the constraint. Under what circumstances would that reasoning be wrong — that is, when should a team pursue stage optimisation even though the optimistic scenario fails the unit-economics test?

Question 2 Meera added a stage whose denominator is capacity rather than demand. What else in Onkar's reporting must change for that stage to be read correctly, and what new pathology does a capacity denominator invite?

Question 3 Omkara Intelligence's forced-activation flow moved its target metric by twenty-eight points and damaged the business. If you had been in the October review that approved it, what single question would have been most likely to stop it, and why is that question so rarely asked?

13. Going deeper

CAC, LTV and payback. Stage rates are the factors from which both CAC and LTV are assembled; without them, a payback period is an assertion rather than a decomposition, and cannot be acted on.

Constructing a funnel. The instrumentation work that makes stage measurement possible — event schemas, identity resolution, boundary definitions — and the place where most of the errors in this note are originally introduced.

Measuring product marketing. Extends stage discipline to message and positioning: whether the reason people moved between stages was the thing you said, which requires message-level rather than channel-level instrumentation.

Growth loops vs funnels. The live theoretical alternative set out in section 10; essential for understanding why a funnel systematically undercounts compounding and what replaces it in businesses where output feeds input.

Building a growth model. Turns the stage rates into a forward projection with explicit assumptions, which is what converts the bounded-prize calculation from a one-off analysis into a planning instrument.

Acquisition channels and economics. Where the mix effects of Table 3 and the incrementality results of section 4 originate; a stage model without a channel model will keep producing paradoxes it cannot explain.

Activation and onboarding optimisation. The deepest single well of headroom in most consumer funnels, and the place where the selection-versus-causation trap of section 8 does the most damage.

Engagement loops and habit. Supplies the mechanism behind the retention curves in Figure 3, and explains why the asymptote rather than the day-30 point is the quantity that determines lifetime value.

Retention strategy. The discipline that operates on the narrow end of the funnel, where economic weight is highest and statistical resolution is lowest — and therefore where judgement matters most.

Savera Fresh Networks: The Cost of a Stranger

A decision case on metrics by funnel stage. The case does not resolve.

1. The night before

At a quarter past eleven on the night of Sunday, 4 October 2026, Shalini Bhatt was still at the dining table of her flat in Jubilee Hills, Hyderabad, with three printouts before her and a fourth she had not opened. At nine the next morning the board of Savera Fresh Networks would approve the winter growth plan: thirty crore rupees of marketing across October 2026 to March 2027, the largest commitment the company had made. Media inventory for the Diwali fortnight locked on Wednesday, 7 October; Diwali fell on 8 November.

The three printouts did not agree. The first, from Suhasini Menon in Bengaluru, showed a quarter in which Savera had put ten lakh new app installs at the top of its funnel for eight crore forty lakh rupees of paid media, the cheapest installs in the company's history. The second, from Sarthak Rane in Toronto, read the same quarter from the bottom: of those ten lakh installs, 38,244 were expected to be taking a delivery ninety days later, and the channel producing the cheapest install produced the dearest one of those. The third, from Swati Ranganathan, the chief financial officer, showed 61,180 new paying subscribers in the billing system, not 65,550.

The email she had not opened was from Yashodhara Pillai in Singapore. The subject line read: Before tomorrow — we are measuring the wrong end of the business.

2. The company, and a decision made in 2022

Savera Fresh Networks was founded in Hyderabad in 2020 by Bhatt, formerly a supply-chain manager at a large listed dairy, and Yash Deshmukh, an operations engineer. The product is a subscription: farm-chilled cow's milk in a returnable bottle delivered before six in the morning, with curd, paneer, eggs and bread in the same basket, paid from a prepaid wallet on a UPI AutoPay mandate. At 31 August 2026 it served four cities and, on finance's definition, 1,86,400 active subscribers spending an average of ₹1,780 a month: ₹33.18 crore of revenue a month, an annualised ₹398 crore, on which Savera earns ₹310 of contribution per active subscriber per month, or 17.4 per cent, after milk, cold chain, packaging, spoilage and the last mile.

Two decisions taken in 2022 shape everything available to Bhatt in 2026. The first was a five-year exclusive supply agreement with a Telangana producer company for chilled raw milk at a formula price, carrying a minimum daily offtake of 1.62 lakh litres, any shortfall billed at 60 per cent of that price. Savera draws 1.71 lakh litres a day. The second was to refuse the gig model: the milkmen are on fixed retainers, on routes the company owns, which makes service quality unusually good and makes the cost of a delivery a function of how many houses on a route are customers. Below roughly forty-five drops per route per day, a route loses money. Together the two mean Savera cannot shrink gracefully and cannot grow thinly.

3. The industry

Indian packaged milk is dominated by co-operatives and large private dairies — Amul, Mother Dairy, Heritage Foods, Dodla Dairy — whose distribution is the local shop. The subscription segment Savera occupies, pioneered at scale by Country Delight, sells not milk but the absence of the errand. Its customers are dual-income households in gated communities, whose alternative is not another subscription but a two-minute walk — and since 2024 Zepto, Blinkit and Swiggy Instamart have stocked chilled milk in dark stores at ten-minute delivery, below Savera's prices, with no commitment and no bottle to return. FSSAI licensing and the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 both bear on the business; a re-consent exercise in January 2026 cut the base Savera could lawfully contact by about a fifth. The 2025 Series C was led by Yashovan Capital Partners of Singapore, which holds two board seats.

4. What happened, and what has since turned out to be wrong

Until March 2026 Savera's weekly growth review opened with one number: app installs. It was legible, daily, and Menon's team was very good at moving it. In April prices rose about seven per cent to cover a milk formula revision. In May, Svenja Bauer in Berlin shipped an onboarding flow that moved address capture ahead of payment, on evidence that it lifted first-order completion. In June the growth budget was raised, and Meta and Google absorbed most of the increase.

By August the install number was excellent and the subscriber number was not. case20v1-growth.funnel.metrics:
Nivesh Saathi Wealth: Counting the Wrong Stage

A decision case on metrics by funnel stage

1. Opening

On the morning of Monday, 14 September 2026, Rohini Iyer sat in a glass meeting room in Indore with a printed dashboard and a deadline. The festive campaign for Nivesh Saathi Wealth, the mutual-fund investing app she had co-founded, would begin with Navratri in the second week of October. Media agencies wanted their bookings locked by Friday, 18 September. The board had approved ₹4 crore for the Diwali quarter, up from ₹2.4 crore in the quarter just ended, and she had to decide how it would be split.

The dashboard's headline number was installs, and it was healthy. Her VP of Growth had a target of 6,00,000 installs for the festive quarter and a plan that met it. A message had arrived overnight from the company's data scientist in Toronto, and it began, "I don't think installs are telling us which money is working."

2. Company background

Nivesh Saathi Wealth was founded in 2019 by Iyer and a classmate, and is headquartered in Indore. It sells one thing: a habit. Users open a zero-commission direct mutual fund account, complete their KYC, and set up a monthly systematic investment plan (SIP) through UPI AutoPay, the NPCI mandate rail. The company is a SEBI-registered distributor of direct plans and earns a platform fee, which the finance team puts at a contribution of ₹60 per active SIP per month after payment and servicing costs.

By August 2026 the app had about 3.1 lakh active SIP accounts with an average instalment of ₹2,100, or roughly ₹65.1 crore of new money a month. Contribution across the base came to ₹1.86 crore a month. The category is crowded. Groww and Zerodha's Coin are the scale players, Paytm Money and ET Money compete for the same salaried first-time investor, and AMFI data shows industry SIP inflows well above ₹25,000 crore a month. Nivesh Saathi's users are mostly first-time investors in tier-2 cities such as Bhopal, Nagpur and Coimbatore.

3. The situation

The growth reporting had been built in the first year, when the only question was whether anyone would download the app. The weekly review therefore opened with installs and cost per install, and every marketing bonus was tied to the install target. Nikhil Joshi, the VP of Growth, had run that system well. In the quarter ended 31 August, paid channels delivered 3,00,000 installs for ₹2.4 crore, a blended cost of ₹80 per install, and organic search and word of mouth added 1,00,000 more.

Neha Raghavan, the data scientist in Toronto, had spent August rebuilding the funnel by stage, rather than by channel-level install counts. Exhibit 1 shows what she found. Of 4,00,000 installs, 1,20,000 users completed KYC, 42,000 set up a first SIP, and based on how each channel's earlier cohorts behaved, about 27,110 would still be investing at month six. Only one install in ten became an investor, and fewer than two in three of those would stay.

Her second cut, Exhibit 2, split the paid channels by spend, and it unsettled the room. Performance advertising on Meta and Google was the cheapest source of installs at ₹60 each, yet the most expensive source of investors: ₹1,091 for each first SIP and ₹2,424 for each SIP still running at month six. Against a contribution of ₹60 a month, a performance-acquired first SIP would take about 18 months to repay its cost, before any drop-out. Partnerships with chartered accountants and employer payroll desks cost ₹150 per install, more than twice as much, but ₹357 per first SIP, and would repay in about six months.

Distance shaped how the team read this. Raghavan, nine and a half hours behind Indore, had sent her analysis at the end of her evening and would sleep through most of Indore's day. Nandini Rao, the product designer in Berlin, pointed out that the KYC screens she had redesigned lost 78 per cent of performance-ad users but only 30 per cent of partner-referred ones, suggesting the problem was intent rather than friction. In Singapore, Ravi Nambiar, who ran partnerships, warned that his channels scaled slowly: a payroll desk took two months to onboard.

Exhibit 3. Decision timeline for the festive quarter.

4. The people

Rohini Iyer, co-founder and chief executive, Indore, must answer to a board that wants growth in active SIPs, not in downloads, but also fears a quiet quarter before the festive peak. Nikhil Joshi, VP of Growth, Indore, owns the 6,00,000-install target and a bonus tied to it. He argues that installs feed every later stage. Neha Raghavan, data scientist, Toronto, wants marketing measured at the stage where money is earned, though her month-6 figures rest on older, smaller cohorts. Ravi Nambiar, head of partnerships, Singapore, wants capital for the channels that work but knows they cannot absorb it quickly.

5. The options

Iyer laid out three courses of action, projected in Exhibit 4 at the unit rates of Exhibit 2.

Option A, buy the install target. Put ₹3 crore into performance advertising and spread ₹1 crore across the rest. The install target would be exceeded, with about 5,83,333 paid installs plus organic. Its cost is that 75 per cent of the budget goes to the channel with the highest cost per retained SIP, and it assumes festive auction prices on Meta and Google do not rise.

Option B, rebalance to retained SIPs. Cut performance advertising to ₹80 lakh and put ₹1.6 crore into creators and ₹80 lakh each into partnerships and referrals. It offers the lowest cost per retained SIP, but assumes channels now absorbing ₹30 lakh to ₹60 lakh can each take ₹80 lakh to ₹1.6 crore at the same efficiency. Nambiar doubts that, and installs, at 4,00,000 paid plus 1,00,000 organic, would fall a sixth short of Joshi's target.

Option C, stage-gated release. Commit ₹3 crore now, with ₹1.2 crore to performance, ₹1 crore to creators, ₹50 lakh to partners and ₹30 lakh to referrals, and hold ₹1 crore until a stage-level read at day 14 of the campaign. It costs install volume and needs a working dashboard by early October, but it limits spending on assumptions.

6. Questions for discussion

  1. Using Exhibits 1 and 2, at which funnel stage is each channel efficient or wasteful, and which single metric would you have used to compare the channels?
  2. Why did cost per install and cost per retained SIP rank the channels in opposite order? What does each measure at its own stage?
  3. Which assumptions in Exhibit 4 are you least willing to rely on, and how would you test them within the campaign itself?
  4. Joshi's bonus depends on installs. What should Iyer change in the way the team is measured, and when?

7. A note for the learner

Stage metrics answer different questions. Installs measure awareness, KYC completion measures interest, first SIP measures transaction and month-6 continuation measures loyalty. Spend should be judged at the latest stage the data can support, because early metrics reward cheap volume. Here the channel with the lowest cost per install had the highest cost per retained SIP.

One defensible path is Option C. Option A optimises the stage that is easiest to count. Option B follows the evidence but extrapolates far beyond the range Exhibit 2 supports. Option C shifts spend toward the stronger channels, keeps enough performance advertising to hold the funnel's top open, and preserves ₹1 crore to be released by the evidence rather than the plan. Iyer would also reset the growth target from installs to first SIPs and month-6 retained SIPs. Its weakness is that day 14 is early for a loyalty judgement, so first-SIP rates and the second successful UPI AutoPay debit should stand in as leading indicators.

Metrics by Funnel Stage

What should a growth leader measure at each point between a stranger noticing the brand and a customer coming back on their own — and why does one aggregate number never answer that question?

A board meeting on the ninth of February

On the morning of 9 February 2026, Ananya Kulkarni stood in the tenth-floor boardroom of Firdaus Mart's Pune headquarters with a single slide open on the screen behind her. Firdaus Mart was a three-year-old quick-commerce grocery app competing for the same fifteen-minute-delivery customer that Blinkit, Zepto and Swiggy Instamart were chasing across urban India, and Ananya, as the company's VP of Growth, had been asked to defend a proposed ₹42 crore growth budget for the financial year beginning in April. The slide showed two lines. The first was app installs, which had grown 41 percent quarter over quarter after a festive-season campaign the company ran through October and November 2025. The second was net revenue, which had grown 6 percent over the same period — inside the range that could be explained by seasonality alone. Rajat Mehra, the board's independent director and a former CFO of a listed retail chain, asked the question everyone in the room was thinking: if the top of the funnel is growing this fast, where is the money going?

It was not an idle question, and the stakes attached to Ananya's answer were concrete. If she told the board that Firdaus Mart simply needed more of the same marketing spend to convert installs into revenue, and she was wrong, the company would compound a problem rather than fix it, burning another ₹42 crore acquiring customers who behaved exactly like the last cohort. If she told the board the growth engine itself was broken and she was wrong, she would needlessly starve a channel that was working. The only way to answer Rajat's question honestly was to stop talking about "the funnel" as a single number and instead ask, stage by stage, what each part of the customer's journey was actually doing — and that discipline, matching the right measurement to the right stage, is the subject of this reading.

The idea: a different question for every stage

Metrics by funnel stage is the practice of choosing distinct, stage-appropriate measures for each phase of a customer's journey — awareness, interest, transaction and loyalty — rather than reporting one blended number and asking it to explain the whole business. The reason this matters is not aesthetic. It is that the actions which move a metric at one stage frequently have no effect, or a perverse effect, on the metric at the next stage. A more eye-catching advertisement raises awareness; it says nothing about whether the product, once tried, is good enough to be bought again. A steep first-order discount raises transaction-stage conversion; it can simultaneously depress loyalty, because it recruits price-sensitive shoppers who were never going to return once the discount lapsed. Treat the funnel as one number and these two effects cancel each other out in a spreadsheet while quietly destroying the business.

The idea has two intellectual parents. The older one is the marketing funnel itself, formalised as AIDA — Attention, Interest, Desire, Action — by the American advertising writer Elias St. Elmo Lewis around 1898, to describe how a stranger becomes a buyer through a sequence of distinct mental states. The newer one is the "Pirate Metrics" framework — Acquisition, Activation, Retention, Referral, Revenue, or AARRR — proposed by the investor and growth practitioner Dave McClure in 2007, while advising early-stage technology companies at 500 Startups. McClure's contribution was to move the funnel out of the advertising department and into the product itself: activation and retention are not marketing outcomes, they are product outcomes, measured by what a user does inside the app in the days after signup. Contemporary growth practice, of the kind taught in the digital-first electives at INSEAD, HKUST and Cambridge, fuses the two lineages: an awareness-to-interest-to-transaction sequence borrowed from AIDA, sitting on top of an activation-to-retention-to-referral engine borrowed from McClure, with the whole system read as flows of people rather than a static picture. If Ananya needed one sentence to carry into the boardroom, it was this: because a fix that helps one stage of the funnel can actively damage the next one, each stage is measured on its own terms, and only afterward are the stages added up.

How it actually works

The mechanics begin with a decision that looks trivial and is not: naming the stages precisely for the business at hand. For Firdaus Mart, Ananya defined four — Awareness (a person becomes aware the app exists), Interest (that person engages enough to install and open it), Transaction (that person completes a paid order), and Loyalty (that person orders again without being re-acquired). Every subsequent step depends on these boundaries being drawn the same way by every team that reports a number, because a metric named "conversion rate" is meaningless until everyone agrees where the stage it describes begins and ends — a discipline that connects directly to the earlier work of constructing the funnel itself as an instrumented pipeline of events.

The second step is to select, for each stage, a small number of metrics — usually two to four — that isolate what that stage alone is responsible for, plus one rate that connects it to the stage before it. Awareness is measured by reach and impressions on the input side, and by unaided or aided brand recall and branded search volume on the output side — the number of people who, having seen the brand, later typed "Firdaus Mart" into a search bar unprompted. Interest is measured by click-through rate, app installs, sign-ups and the interest-to-transaction conversion rate that ties it forward. Transaction is measured by checkout completion rate, average order value and cost per acquired customer. Loyalty is measured by repeat-purchase rate at fixed windows — commonly day 7, day 30 and day 90 — alongside churn, referral rate and lifetime value. The point of keeping the list short is that a stage with fifteen tracked metrics has, in practice, no owner and no decision rule; a stage with three has both.

The third step, the one practitioners most often leave implicit, is instrumenting the boundary between each pair of stages so that a single user's movement from one to the next can actually be traced with a timestamp and an identifier — an install that cannot be linked to the campaign that produced it, or a first order that cannot be linked to the install that preceded it, breaks the entire chain and forces the team back onto blended, unstage-able numbers. The fourth step is baselining: each stage-to-stage conversion rate needs to be observed over a period long enough to average out weekly noise — a single bad Tuesday means little, four consecutive weeks of decline means a great deal. The fifth step, and the one that turns stage metrics from a reporting exercise into a decision tool, is using them to decompose the two summary numbers the board actually cares about: customer acquisition cost and lifetime value, each of which is simply the arithmetic product of the stage-to-stage rates that came before it. That decomposition is what Ananya turned to next.

The worked example: where Firdaus Mart's ₹40 lakh went

Firdaus Mart's festive-season campaign, which ran through October and November 2025, spent ₹40,00,000 to reach an audience across paid social and search. Table 1 shows what happened to that spend as it moved through the four stages, and Figure 1 shows the same sequence as a funnel.

Reading the funnel this way already tells Ananya something a single "conversion rate" would have hidden: the campaign moved 2 crore impressions down to 36,000 paying customers, a blended conversion of 0.18 percent, a figure that on its own says nothing about which of the three intermediate rates — click-through, install-to-order, or repeat-purchase — was the one worth fixing. The arithmetic in Table 1 makes the stakes explicit by turning those stage rates into the two numbers the board actually voted on: customer acquisition cost and lifetime value.
